blocks.text: Prompt engineering and fine-tuning are the two most common ways to make a general purpose model behave the way you actually need it to, and they work by fundamentally different mechanisms.

Prompt engineering shapes behavior at call time, through the instructions and examples included in each request. Fine-tuning shapes behavior once, ahead of time, by adjusting the model weights themselves. Knowing when each one earns its cost is one of the most practical decisions in building an AI product.
1. Two Different Ways to Change Model Behavior

Both approaches aim at the same outcome, a model that behaves the way your application needs, but they intervene at different points, prompting intervenes at request time, fine-tuning intervenes at training time.
This distinction matters because it drives almost every other tradeoff between the two approaches, iteration speed, cost structure, consistency, and how much data each one actually requires.
2. Prompt Engineering, Instructions at Call Time

blocks.alt: Instructions sent with every call shape model behavior

blocks.text: Prompt engineering works by carefully crafting the instructions, examples, and context sent to the model on every single call. The model weights never change, only the input changes.
This makes prompting flexible and instantly reversible, you can change your entire approach between one call and the next simply by editing the text you send, with no retraining required.
3. Fine-Tuning, Behavior Baked Into Weights

blocks.alt: Training examples adjust the weights once, producing built-in behavior

blocks.text: Fine-tuning works by running a training process on a dataset of examples, adjusting the model weights so the desired behavior becomes the model default, without needing to be re-explained on every call.
Once training finishes, that behavior is fixed until the model is fine-tuned again, changing it requires a new training run, not just a text edit.
4. Iteration Speed, Prompting Wins Easily

blocks.alt: A prompt is edited and tested immediately

blocks.text: Prompt changes can be tested in seconds, edit the text, send the request, read the response. This tight feedback loop makes prompting the natural starting point for almost any new task.

Fine-tuning cannot match that speed. Even a fast fine-tuning run takes minutes to hours, plus the time needed to collect and prepare training data beforehand, so iterating on a fine-tuning approach is inherently slower.

blocks.alt: Fine-tuning requires collecting data, training a model, then evaluating it

blocks.text: 5. Consistency, Fine-Tuning Wins Reliably
Prompting relies on the model correctly interpreting instructions fresh on every call, which introduces some variability, especially for subtle behaviors or unusual formats.
Fine-tuning bakes the target behavior directly into the weights, so consistency tends to be noticeably higher once training is done well, an advantage that grows as request volume grows.

blocks.text: 6. Cost Per Call vs Upfront Cost

blocks.alt: A prompted approach costs more tokens per call while a fine-tuned approach carries an upfront training cost

blocks.text: A heavily prompted approach, with long instructions and several examples baked into every request, pays a token cost on every single call, which adds up quickly at high volume.

A fine-tuned model shifts that cost forward, an upfront training expense, in exchange for a much shorter prompt and lower per call cost afterward. At high enough volume, that tradeoff usually favors fine-tuning.

blocks.title: The crossover point is a real calculation
blocks.content: Whether fine-tuning saves money depends on request volume, prompt length saved, and training cost, a calculation worth doing explicitly rather than assuming either direction by default.

blocks.text: 7. Combining Both, Not an Either Or Choice

blocks.alt: Prompting and fine-tuning combine into one system

blocks.text: In practice, most production systems use both. A fine-tuned model handles the core, stable behavior of the task, while prompting still supplies request specific details, user context, or instructions that change from call to call.
Fine-tuning a model does not remove the ability to prompt it, the fine-tuned model still accepts a prompt, it simply starts from a more aligned default than a general purpose model would.

code.content:
# A fine-tuned model still accepts prompt level detail on top
# of its baked-in default behavior
response = fine_tuned_support_model.generate(
    "Customer message: " + user_message +
    "\nAccount tier: " + account_tier
)

blocks.text: 8. A Decision Table

blocks.alt: Frequently changing task definitions point toward prompting rather than fine-tuning

blocks.text: A simple starting question helps guide the decision, does the exact behavior you need change often. If yes, prompting is usually the better fit, since it can adapt instantly. If the behavior is stable and repeated at high volume, fine-tuning becomes worth considering.

items: Task definition still evolving, prompt first and iterate quickly
Task is stable and repeated at high volume, fine-tuning likely pays off
Need instant behavior changes based on user or session context, keep that part in the prompt
Need strict, repeatable format or tone at scale, fine-tuning tends to be more reliable

blocks.text: Worked Example
A startup building a code review assistant starts entirely with prompt engineering, iterating on the wording of instructions daily as they learn what kind of feedback developers actually find useful.

After three months, the review style has stabilized, developers consistently want the same categories of feedback in the same format. The team collects two thousand examples of their now stable review style and fine-tunes a smaller model on it, cutting both prompt length and per call cost while keeping quality steady.
They keep a short prompt on top of the fine-tuned model for repository specific context, combining both approaches rather than choosing one permanently over the other.
Common Mistakes

items: Jumping straight to fine-tuning before the task definition has stabilized through prompting first
Treating fine-tuning and prompting as mutually exclusive, when most production systems use both together
Underestimating how much longer the fine-tuning iteration loop is compared to editing a prompt
Ignoring the token cost savings a fine-tuned model can unlock once request volume is high

blocks.text: Practice

Take a prompt you currently use in production or in a personal project. Estimate how many tokens of that prompt exist purely to force consistent behavior, then imagine what a fine-tuned version of that same task might look like with a much shorter prompt.
Key Takeaway

Prompt engineering changes behavior instantly through the request itself, while fine-tuning changes behavior permanently through the model weights, and most mature systems end up combining both rather than relying on either one alone.
